newsitem.title: USA: Junk telecomm sector shines, U.S. corporates slow.
newsitem.headline: Junk telecomm sector shines, U.S. corporates slow.

text.p: Amid a generally slow day in the U.S. corporate bond market, high-yield telecommunications debt continued to chalk up gains as a result of excitement generated by last week's announcement of the merger between MCI Corp and British Telecom, traders said.
"There's been a dramatic sea-change in investor perception in the recent week. There's a feeling that M&A activity is back in the market," said one trader.
Zero coupon bonds such as Brooks Fiber Properties Inc, ICG Holdings Inc and Intermedia Communications Inc increased by 1/2 to 3/4 of a point in today's trading, traders said.
In the broader markets, investment-grade debt generally traded in line with Treasuries.
The price of the benchmark Treasury was up by one point to yield 6.59 percent.
Traders said high-yield bonds were up by 1/8 to 1/4 of a point, but still lagged the gains made in the Treasury market.
One trader speculated that secondary trading was sluggish in the junk market becuase investors were focusing on the heavy new issue forward calendar.
"Customers are focused on the 22 deals in the pipeline. That's making the secondary market fairly lackluster."
Two issuers, both in oil and gas sector, caught investor attention on Tuesday by selling a large amount of junk bonds in 144a private placement offerings.
Abraxas Petroleum debuted in the junk market with the sale of $215 million in 11 1/2 percent B2/single-B notes due 2004 via BT Securities.
Sources say the deal was upgrade to $215 million from $200 million as a result of very high buy-side demand, sources said.
Also, Parker Drilling Co sold $300 million in B1/B-plus senior notes due 2006 through Jeffries & Co.
In the investment-grade arena, Associates Corp of North America, a unit of Ford Motor Co, sold $300 million in 6.875 percent A1/A-plus rated subordinated notes due 2008 via Salomon Brothers.
Early on Tuesday, CIT Group Holdings sold $100 million of 5.875 percent AA3/A-plus rated notes due 1992 through Lehman Brothers.
